paragraphs: A learning algorithm produces a prediction function, and a central theoretical question is how its performance on training data relates to performance beyond that data. This paper approaches that question through hypothesis stability: a measure of stability expressed directly in the normed space containing the functions the algorithm can output.

The main contribution is a general bound connecting generalization error to this form of stability. Measuring stability at the level of the output function makes the function space itself part of the analysis. The proof uses martingale inequalities in a Banach space, providing mathematical tools for controlling fluctuations of quantities that take values in that space.

The authors then apply their general bounds to particular learning algorithms based on empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent. These applications show how the framework can support analysis of familiar learning procedures. The result supplies a way to bound generalization through hypothesis stability; it does not claim that every algorithm automatically has favorable stability.
icml-2017-algorithmic-stability-and-hypo.tldr: The paper bounds generalization error through stability measured directly in the function space of a learning algorithm’s outputs.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs contain entities connected by different kinds of relations. Multi-relational embedding learns hidden representations of both, with the aim of supporting inference over these connections. This paper asks how those representations can be organized around analogical properties, making relationships among entities and relations part of the learning objective.

The proposed framework optimizes embeddings with respect to those analogical properties using a differentiable objective. Differentiability gives the framework a computational route for learning the representations, and the authors describe the resulting model as scalable. The central contribution is therefore an explicit principle for organizing embeddings, together with an optimization formulation that can implement it.

On benchmark datasets, the model significantly outperformed many representative baseline methods. The paper also proves that several established multi-relational embedding methods are special cases of its framework. That unification gives the proposal theoretical value alongside its empirical results: it connects existing approaches under a broader formulation rather than presenting only another isolated embedding model.
icml-2017-analogical-inference-for-multi.tldr: A differentiable framework learns knowledge-graph embeddings around analogical properties and unifies several existing embedding methods.

paragraphs: Some networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions: their connection counts include a substantial tail of highly connected nodes. This paper develops a random simple-graph model designed to capture power-law degree behavior. It constructs edge probabilities using Bertoin–Fujita–Roynette–Yor random variables, whose distribution provides the mechanism for producing the desired tail.

The construction can also represent latent factors in a way similar to stochastic block models while retaining its power-law degree distribution. This allows hidden network structure and heavy-tailed connectivity to coexist in one model. Rather than fixing the precise power-law behavior in advance, the method learns parameters of the underlying random-variable distribution through probabilistic inference.

For computation, the authors use gamma approximations to the BFRY variables within variational Bayesian inference. They apply this procedure to network datasets where power-law degrees are a natural assumption. To improve scalability further, they estimate gradients from subsets of graph edges and use stochastic gradient ascent, connecting a flexible probabilistic construction with an inference procedure suited to larger networks.
icml-2017-bayesian-inference-on-random-s.tldr: A Bayesian graph model learns power-law connectivity from data while accommodating latent structure and minibatch inference.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks can improve prediction, but independently training them and then averaging or voting leaves their collaboration largely unstructured. This paper introduces confident multiple choice learning, or CMCL, as an ensemble method designed specifically for deep networks. It builds on multiple choice learning while addressing an overconfidence issue in that approach.

CMCL changes three parts of the ensemble: its objective, architecture, and training procedure. These components are a confident oracle loss, feature sharing, and stochastic labeling. Together, they make collaboration part of how the models are trained, rather than relying solely on a final aggregation of independently learned predictions.

The authors evaluate CMCL on image classification using CIFAR and SVHN and on foreground-background segmentation using iCoseg. With five residual networks, CMCL reduces top-1 classification error relative to the corresponding independent ensemble by 14.05% on CIFAR and 6.60% on SVHN. These are relative error reductions, supporting the benefits of coordinated ensemble learning in the reported experiments.
icml-2017-confident-multiple-choice-lear.tldr: CMCL addresses overconfidence in multiple choice learning through a new loss, feature sharing, and stochastic labeling, improving reported ensemble results.

paragraphs: Momentum can change how an optimization method moves, but understanding its behavior is harder when the objective is nonsmooth and nonconvex. This paper studies accelerated proximal gradient for nonconvex programming, called APGnc. At each iteration, it compares a standard proximal gradient candidate with a linear extrapolation candidate and accepts the one with the lower objective value.

This selection produces a monotonic decrease in the objective. The authors prove that limit points of the generated sequence are critical points under their general nonsmooth, nonconvex setting. They then use the Kurdyka–Lojasiewicz property to establish linear and sublinear rates for objective values across a broad class of functions. These guarantees concern critical points, without asserting global optimality.

The paper also introduces a stochastic variance-reduced version and proves linear convergence under a special case of that property. Further analysis covers inexact versions of the methods. An adaptive momentum strategy improves numerical performance, connecting the convergence analysis to a practical choice about how aggressively to extrapolate.
icml-2017-convergence-analysis-of-proxim.tldr: The paper establishes conditional convergence guarantees for proximal gradient methods that compare momentum steps against ordinary updates.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations becomes more complicated when several agents act together. An individual action can depend on the agent’s role within a shared strategy, yet demonstrations may never explicitly identify those roles. This paper treats coordination as hidden structure that must be inferred alongside the behavior of each agent.

The proposed approach jointly learns a latent coordination model and individual policies. It combines unsupervised structure learning, which discovers the hidden organization of the demonstrations, with conventional imitation learning, which learns how agents behave. Joint learning makes the inferred coordination part of the same modeling process as the policies it is meant to support.

The authors demonstrate the approach in team sports, where players occupy different roles within a coordinated strategy and fine-grained behavior is difficult to model. Inferring player roles through the coordination model substantially improves imitation loss compared with conventional baselines. This finding supports the value of modeling hidden roles when learning demonstrated team behavior; the reported measure concerns imitation quality.
icml-2017-coordinated-multi-agent-imitat.tldr: Jointly learning hidden coordination and individual policies improves imitation of team-sport behavior in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Transferring a neural network from one domain to another requires representations that remain useful when the data distribution changes. This paper introduces joint adaptation networks, or JAN, to address that problem. Its central idea is to align the joint distributions of several domain-specific layers across the source and target domains.

The alignment criterion is joint maximum mean discrepancy, abbreviated JMMD. Considering multiple layers jointly makes their combined distribution the object of adaptation. The method also uses adversarial training to maximize JMMD, making differences between source and target distributions more distinguishable. This supplies a stronger discrepancy signal for the network’s distribution-alignment task.

The authors describe learning through stochastic gradient descent, with gradients computed by back-propagation in linear time. This connects the joint-distribution criterion to a practical neural-network training procedure. Experiments on standard datasets achieve results reported as state of the art. The findings support joint adaptation as an effective transfer-learning approach in those evaluations, alongside a computational formulation compatible with gradient-based training.
icml-2017-deep-transfer-learning-with-jo.tldr: Joint adaptation networks align distributions across multiple layers, using an adversarial discrepancy criterion to improve domain transfer.

paragraphs: Sequences and graphs have structure that a neural architecture needs to handle. Architecture design often relies on experimental intuition about suitable operations. This paper develops a more formal route: start from kernels over structured objects and use them to derive neural operations appropriate for those objects.

The authors introduce deep recurrent operations and characterize their associated kernel spaces mathematically. Each recurrent module compares an input with virtual reference objects through a kernel. These reference objects play a role analogous to filters in convolutional networks: they are parameterized and learned directly through end-to-end training. The architecture therefore combines a kernel-based interpretation with adaptable neural components.

The proposed architectures are evaluated on language modeling and molecular graph regression, with results reported as state of the art across these applications. Those findings show that the formal construction can also produce competitive predictive models. The broader contribution is a connection between structured similarity functions and trainable recurrent operations, giving architecture design an explicit mathematical starting point.
icml-2017-deriving-neural-architectures-.tldr: The paper derives trainable recurrent neural operations from sequence and graph kernels and reports strong results on both types of data.

paragraphs: Training sparse linear predictors can be costly when a dataset contains both many observations and many features. This paper tackles sparse empirical risk minimization by reformulating the objective as a convex-concave saddle-point problem. That representation exposes both primal and dual variables, giving the optimizer two places where sparsity can reduce work.

The proposed Doubly Greedy Primal-Dual Coordinate Descent algorithm exploits sparsity in both sets of variables and has a low cost per iteration. The theoretical analysis establishes linear convergence with favorable iteration complexity provided the primal variable set is sparse. This condition matters: the convergence statement is explicitly tied to the sparse setting analyzed by the authors.

An extension uses active sets to make the algorithm faster still. Experiments on large-scale multiclass datasets report speedups of up to thirtyfold over several state-of-the-art optimization methods. Together, the results connect inexpensive individual updates, a conditional convergence guarantee, and substantial observed acceleration on the tested problems.
icml-2017-doubly-greedy-primal-dual-coor.tldr: A primal-dual coordinate method exploits sparsity on both sides of the optimization problem, with conditional linear convergence and reported speedups up to thirtyfold.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks need practical approximations to estimate uncertainty. Dropout variational inference is one such approach, but its objective can lead to severe underestimation of model uncertainty. Alpha-divergences offer alternatives that can avoid this problem, although existing implementations described by the authors require Gaussian approximations and substantial changes to models.

The paper reparameterizes alpha-divergence objectives to make them easier to use with dropout. The resulting inference technique can be implemented in existing models by changing the loss function. This matters because it makes a different treatment of uncertainty accessible through the training objective, without requiring the radical model changes associated with the earlier techniques.

Experiments show improved accuracy and uncertainty estimates compared with variational inference in dropout networks. The authors also examine epistemic uncertainty away from the data using adversarial images. In that study, model uncertainty distinguishes adversarial from non-adversarial images. This is evidence about the uncertainty behavior of the evaluated model, rather than a universal guarantee of adversarial detection.
icml-2017-dropout-inference-in-bayesian-.tldr: A reparameterized alpha-divergence loss makes dropout-based Bayesian inference practical and improves reported accuracy and uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Iterative hard thresholding is a projected-gradient approach to optimization with sparsity constraints. Existing methods discussed in this paper operate on the primal minimization problem. The authors investigate whether a dual formulation can provide another route through a setting that is nonconvex and NP-hard.

For sparsity-constrained objectives with squared-norm regularization, they establish a duality theory giving necessary and sufficient conditions for equivalent solution in dual space. They then propose dual iterative hard thresholding, a supergradient method for maximizing the nonsmooth dual objective. The equivalence is conditional, so the theory does not make arbitrary sparse optimization problems easy.

The analysis finds that dual IHT’s sparse recovery performance is invariant to the Restricted Isometry Property, which the authors identify as required by existing primal IHT methods without sparsity relaxation. A stochastic variant addresses larger-scale optimization. Numerical results show more accurate model estimation with small training datasets and greater computational efficiency than the compared state-of-the-art primal IHT algorithms.
icml-2017-dual-iterative-hard-thresholdi.tldr: The paper establishes conditional sparse duality and develops dual hard-thresholding algorithms with favorable recovery and computational results.

paragraphs: MAP inference seeks the most likely configuration of states in a graphical model. Although this problem is NP-hard in general, large instances can sometimes be solved effectively. This paper offers a sufficient structural condition that helps explain when exact inference can have a polynomial-time guarantee.

The condition concerns a linear-programming relaxation, which admits fractional solutions alongside valid discrete configurations. The authors require that only polynomially many fractional vertices have objective values better than the optimal valid solution. Under that condition, they prove that MAP inference can be performed in polynomial time. The key quantity is therefore the number of fractional competitors that outrank the true optimum.

This resolves an open question identified in the abstract and goes beyond known techniques for general integer-program relaxations, which handle only constantly many such vertices. Experiments verify the proposed condition in the evaluated settings and examine how efficiently integer-programming methods remove fractional solutions. The result provides a conditional explanation of tractability while retaining the problem’s general NP-hardness.
icml-2017-exact-map-inference-by-avoidin.tldr: Exact MAP inference is polynomial-time solvable when only polynomially many fractional relaxation vertices outperform the best valid configuration.

paragraphs: Finding the nearest data points becomes difficult as dimensionality grows. Many exact nearest-neighbor methods have query times that depend exponentially on ambient or intrinsic dimension. Dynamic Continuous Indexing, or DCI, already reduces dependence on intrinsic dimension to a sublinear form. This paper introduces Prioritized DCI to improve that dependence further.

Its central result describes a favorable tradeoff between storage and query difficulty. A linear increase in intrinsic dimensionality, corresponding to an exponential increase in the number of nearby points, can be mostly counteracted by a linear increase in space. The qualification matters: the paper describes largely offsetting the dimensionality increase rather than eliminating its effects entirely.

The empirical evaluation also shows substantial improvements over prior methods. Compared with Locality-Sensitive Hashing, Prioritized DCI requires between fourteen and 116 times fewer distance evaluations and uses twenty-one times less memory. These measurements support the method’s practical efficiency in the reported comparisons, alongside the theoretical improvement in how search responds to intrinsic dimensionality.
icml-2017-fast-k-nearest-neighbour-searc.tldr: Prioritized DCI improves the space-versus-dimensionality tradeoff for nearest-neighbor search and substantially reduces reported distance evaluations and memory use.

paragraphs: A regression loss determines which prediction errors a method treats as costly. This paper introduces a general framework for forest-type regression in which that loss can be selected from a broad family. The flexibility makes it possible to construct forest regressors specifically intended to reduce sensitivity to outliers.

The framework also includes familiar methods: choosing squared-error loss recovers classical random forests, while choosing quantile loss recovers quantile random forests. These connections show how different forest estimators fit within one formulation. The authors then use robust losses to develop additional regressors, making robustness an explicit modeling choice within the same framework.

Experiments with simulated and real data find that the robust forests are substantially less sensitive to outliers. The authors also report that selecting an appropriate number of nearest neighbors can quickly improve random-forest generalization. The findings identify both loss selection and neighborhood size as useful choices in the studied forest methods, with the robustness improvements demonstrated empirically.
icml-2017-forest-type-regression-with-ge.tldr: A general-loss framework unifies familiar forest regressors and produces robust variants that are less sensitive to outliers in experiments.

paragraphs: Sequence-labeling systems often begin with a fixed vocabulary of basic units and a fixed way to divide target sequences into them. In speech recognition, those units might be characters, words, or phonemes. This paper argues that fixing both choices can restrict modeling performance and proposes learning them through the loss function.

Gram-CTC extends the CTC criterion so that the model can learn useful units, called grams, and suitable decompositions of target sequences. It preserves the advantages of CTC while allowing different numbers of characters to be emitted at a time step. This flexibility enables the model to capture longer-term dependencies and improves computational efficiency.

The authors evaluate Gram-CTC on large-vocabulary speech recognition across multiple data scales. They report improvements over CTC in both predictive performance and efficiency, as well as results exceeding the state of the art on a standard speech benchmark. These findings support treating unit selection and target decomposition as learnable parts of sequence modeling.
icml-2017-gram-ctc-automatic-unit-select.tldr: Gram-CTC learns output units and target decompositions, improving reported speech-recognition performance and efficiency over CTC.

paragraphs: Covariance-based dimensionality reduction uses directions estimated from a finite dataset, while the corresponding population directions are unknown. This paper asks when the eigenvectors of a sample covariance matrix reliably reflect those of the actual covariance matrix. The question directly concerns how much data is sufficient for useful estimates.

The authors prove bounds relating inner products between sample and population eigenvectors to sample count and separation between the respective eigenvalues. Greater separation and more samples control overlap across different eigendirections. Their analysis covers a wide family of distributions, including finite-second-moment distributions and sub-Gaussian distributions supported in a centered Euclidean ball.

The resulting concentration bounds apply to both eigenvectors and eigenvalues at finite sample sizes, providing tools for non-asymptotic PCA analysis. In particular, the paper gives conditions under which estimated components can be separated using only a constant number of samples. It also shows that few samples can suffice for dimensionality reduction, especially when the covariance is low rank; these are conditional possibilities rather than universal sample guarantees.
icml-2017-how-close-are-the-eigenvectors.tldr: Finite-sample covariance bounds explain conditions under which PCA directions and useful dimensionality reduction can be recovered from few observations.

paragraphs: Machine teaching asks how to choose examples that help a learner reach a desired model. This paper studies a sequential version in which the learner updates iteratively and the teacher selects examples based on its current performance. The teacher can therefore adapt instruction as learning progresses.

That setup changes the objective compared with constructing a minimal training set for a batch learner. Here, the focus is fast convergence of the evolving learner model. The authors show that teaching complexity differs substantially between iterative and batch settings, so conclusions about a single fixed dataset do not directly settle the sequential teaching problem.

The paper develops teaching algorithms for different levels of information available about the learner. Under the corresponding settings, these algorithms provably reduce the number of teaching examples and speed convergence compared with learning without a teacher. Experiments across different data distributions and real image datasets support the theoretical findings, connecting adaptive example selection to measurable improvements in the learner’s progress.
icml-2017-iterative-machine-teaching-419.tldr: Adaptive, sequential example selection can provably accelerate iterative learning under the teacher-information settings studied.

paragraphs: Infinite Layer Networks integrate over infinitely many nodes in a single hidden layer. Earlier approaches connect learning these networks to kernel methods, making efficient learning possible when a particular integral can be evaluated analytically. This paper develops an online algorithm that avoids relying on that analytic kernel computation.

The broader idea is to use kernels that can be estimated through sampling even when their values cannot be computed efficiently. Random features supply the approximation needed by the learning procedure. This extends the usable setting from access to efficiently calculated kernel values to access to sampled estimates of those values.

The authors provide a regret analysis showing that their algorithm matches the sample complexity of methods with access to kernel values. That is the precise sense in which the proposed approach achieves comparable performance. The result establishes that explicit use of the kernel trick is not necessary for the analyzed learning guarantees, and it gives a route to learning infinite-layer models through random features.
icml-2017-learning-infinite-layer-networ.tldr: An online random-feature algorithm learns infinite-layer networks with sample complexity matching methods that can access kernel values.

paragraphs: Source code and its compiled object code express related computations in different sequences of statements. This paper proposes a neural architecture for learning the correspondence between those sequences at the statement level. Its target is an alignment that links the two representations of the program.

The architecture maps each statement to a representation that depends on its context. It then aligns those vectors through a grid spanning both sequence domains. This combines contextual information about individual statements with an explicit representation of possible cross-sequence correspondences, giving the network a structure for learning how one sequence translates into the other.

Experiments use short C functions, including both artificial examples and human-written code. The model predicts alignments with high accuracy and outperforms the known baselines in those tests. The authors also demonstrate that the architecture can learn graph problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem. That additional result indicates applicability beyond code alignment, while the code experiments specifically establish performance on short functions.
icml-2017-learning-to-align-the-source-c.tldr: A neural architecture aligns source and compiled statements using contextual vectors and a cross-sequence grid, outperforming baselines on short C functions.

paragraphs: Some clustering tasks group data into meaningful classes, making human feedback useful for correcting uncertain assignments. This paper aims to reduce the amount of feedback required when the data follow a union-of-subspaces model. It develops an active method for choosing pairwise queries rather than requesting input without regard to that structure.

The central rule selects points with the smallest margin between estimated subspaces. These points are analogous to examples near a classification boundary. The authors prove that points close to subspace intersections have low margin, linking the query rule to the geometry of ambiguity. Their procedure can follow any subspace clustering algorithm that produces an affinity matrix.

Across several datasets with subspace structure, the method reduces clustering error considerably faster than the compared state-of-the-art active-query algorithms. On other datasets, it remains competitive. The results support using the estimated geometry to prioritize human input, with the strongest reported comparative gains occurring where the subspace model fits the data structure.
icml-2017-leveraging-union-of-subspace-s.tldr: Querying low-margin points between estimated subspaces makes human-guided clustering more efficient on the reported datasets with subspace structure.

paragraphs: Variational Bayesian neural networks learn an approximation to a posterior distribution, making the quality of that approximation important for prediction and uncertainty. This paper offers a way to improve it by reinterpreting multiplicative noise in the network. The noise becomes auxiliary random variables that augment the approximate posterior.

With this interpretation, normalizing flows can make the approximation more expressive. The authors show that the construction remains efficient and straightforward while preserving local reparameterizations and a tractable lower bound. These properties matter together: a richer probability model is useful for learning only if the resulting training objective and computations remain manageable.

Experiments compare the new approximation with classical mean-field inference for Bayesian neural networks. The authors report significant improvements in both predictive accuracy and predictive uncertainty. The contribution thus joins a probabilistic reinterpretation of multiplicative noise with an implementable inference method, and the reported results show benefits for both the predictions themselves and the uncertainty accompanying them.
icml-2017-multiplicative-normalizing-flo.tldr: Treating multiplicative noise as auxiliary variables enables richer flow-based Bayesian approximations with improved reported accuracy and uncertainty.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization separates data into feature and weight matrices whose entries are nonnegative. A difficult question is whether alternating optimization can recover the true features when their weights are strongly correlated. This paper addresses that question, motivated by the prevalence of such correlations in applications.

The authors propose an alternating gradient-descent algorithm and prove recovery of the ground-truth feature matrix with a mild initialization requirement, even in the presence of strong correlations. In many cases of interest, the permitted correlation is of the same order as the highest possible. The guarantee therefore addresses a challenging correlation regime while retaining an explicit initialization condition.

The theoretical analysis also establishes favorable properties including robustness to noise. Experiments on semi-synthetic datasets complement the theory and show advantages over several popular methods in recovering the ground truth. Together, these results support alternating gradient descent as a recovery method in the analyzed setting, beyond merely finding a nonnegative factorization that fits the observations.
icml-2017-provable-alternating-gradient-.tldr: With mild initialization, an alternating gradient method provably recovers nonnegative features despite strong weight correlations.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using available features while learning from the rewards those actions produce. Generalized linear models are useful when rewards are binary, but much prior theory focused on linear reward models. This paper develops upper-confidence-bound algorithms and guarantees for the generalized linear setting.

The main algorithm achieves regret on the order of the square root of d times T, up to logarithmic factors, for d-dimensional features over T rounds. With the number of arms fixed, this matches the minimax lower bound up to those logarithmic terms and improves the best previous result by a square-root-of-d factor. The fixed-arm assumption is part of the stated comparison.

A key technical contribution is a sharp finite-sample confidence bound for maximum-likelihood estimates in generalized linear models. That bound supports decisions that account for uncertainty in estimated rewards. The authors also analyze a simpler, practically useful upper-confidence-bound algorithm and prove optimal regret in certain cases, distinguishing its conditional guarantee from the main result.
icml-2017-provably-optimal-algorithms-fo.tldr: An upper-confidence-bound method achieves near-minimax regret for generalized linear contextual bandits with a fixed number of arms.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient algorithms evolve through discrete, random updates. This paper develops stochastic modified equations as a way to study those updates using continuous-time stochastic differential equations. The approximation is in the weak sense, so the continuous formulation serves as a probabilistic description of the algorithm rather than an assertion that individual trajectories coincide.

The authors use this formulation together with optimal control theory to derive adaptive policies for adjusting hyperparameters. This connects analysis and algorithm design: the continuous description provides a setting in which adjustment rules can be derived, and those rules become part of the stochastic gradient procedure.

The resulting algorithms achieve competitive performance and are reported to remain robust across varying models and datasets. The contribution is therefore both a collection of adaptive methods and a general methodology for understanding and designing stochastic gradient algorithms. Its significance lies in turning a mathematical approximation into actionable training policies, with empirical results supporting the usefulness of that connection.
icml-2017-stochastic-modified-equations-.tldr: Continuous stochastic approximations and optimal control yield adaptive gradient algorithms with competitive performance across varied models and datasets.

paragraphs: Embedding methods can struggle with sparse data because zeros dominate the observations. Practitioners often reduce their influence by downweighting or subsampling them. This paper instead builds a probabilistic explanation for the abundance of zeros into the embedding method itself, extending the exponential-family embedding approach.

In a zero-inflated embedding, an observed zero can have two sources. It may arise from the interactions represented by the embedding, or from a separate process that places probability directly at zero. Fitting this model naturally reduces the influence of zeros on the learned representations, allowing the model to account for sparsity through its generative structure.

The authors evaluate the method on language, movie ratings, shopping histories, and bird-watching logs. Across these data types, they find improved predictive performance over standard approaches and better vector representations of items. The results support explicitly modeling multiple sources of zeros as a useful way to learn from sparse observations, rather than making every zero carry the same modeling weight.
icml-2017-zero-inflated-exponential-fami.tldr: Zero-inflated embeddings model two possible sources of zeros, improving reported predictions and representations across several sparse data types.
